Teaching case · Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation

Aushadhi Direct: nine numbers before Diwali

Shruti Kamath has four days to decide what her company will read every Monday morning, and ₹1.4 crore rides on whether she builds the instrument or the plumbing first.

1. Thursday evening

At 7:40 in the evening on Thursday, 24 September 2026, the eleventh floor of Aushadhi Direct's office in Gachibowli, Hyderabad, was nearly empty. Shruti Kamath, vice-president of product, had three browser windows open on three different dashboards, and a document she had titled “One Page” that was still blank below the heading.

Nine days earlier, at the September operating review, the chief executive Suresh Nadkarni had said something that the leadership group had received in silence. He had asked each of the seven people at the table to write down, on a slip of paper, the company's refill rate for the previous week. Six slips came back with numbers. The numbers were 38 per cent, 29 per cent, 47 per cent, 31 per cent, “about a third”, and 46.7 per cent. His instruction was short: before Diwali, there would be one weekly dashboard for the company, one reading of it, and one set of definitions. Shruti was to circulate the design by Monday, 28 September; the first reading would be on Monday, 5 October; Diwali fell on 8 November, and with it the biggest ordering fortnight of the year.

What made the task uncomfortable was not the absence of data. Aushadhi Direct had a great deal of data. It had sixty-one tiles across three dashboards, four full-time analysts, and a warehouse bill of ₹19 lakh a quarter. What it did not have was any single number that two functions would defend in the same words.

2. The company

Aushadhi Direct was founded in 2019 in Hyderabad by two pharmacists, Suresh Nadkarni and Meenal Rao, and an engineer who had spent four years at Flipkart. It sold prescription and over-the-counter medicines, plus home-collected diagnostic tests, through an Android app and a web store. By September 2026 it served about 14 lakh customers across 74 cities, with annualised gross merchandise value of roughly ₹520 crore — a respectable but clearly second-tier position in a market where Tata 1mg, Apollo 24|7, PharmEasy and Reliance's Netmeds all had deeper capital and wider brand reach.

The company's economics rested on chronic-care refills. Customers on long-term medication for diabetes, hypertension and thyroid conditions ordered every twenty-eight to thirty-five days, and this cohort — a little over a fifth of the customer base — produced 68 per cent of revenue. Acquisition was expensive and the discounting war with the larger players was unwinnable; retention of the chronic cohort was the whole strategy. Payments ran almost entirely on UPI through Razorpay, with about nine per cent cash on delivery in tier-three towns. Prescription medicines required verification by a registered pharmacist before dispatch, which the state drug-control authorities audited and which the company treated as non-negotiable. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act had, in 2025, forced a rebuild of how health data could be viewed internally — a fact that would shortly matter for dashboard access.

Deliveries ran on the company's own rider fleet in nine cities and on third-party logistics partners everywhere else. A corporate-wellness contract signed in March 2026 with an employer benefits programme in Dubai, covering about 18,000 Indian-expatriate employees and worth ₹2.1 crore a year, had added a monthly reporting obligation in a format the client specified.

3. The situation

Shruti had spent the previous week interviewing the readers of each dashboard, and the findings were in Exhibit 1. The growth page, owned by Anand Pillai in Hyderabad, had nineteen tiles and was genuinely read, though mainly for cost per acquired customer. The operations page had twenty-six tiles and was read every morning by the fulfilment team, who ignored twenty-two of them. The care page had sixteen tiles and was read by nobody outside the care function. Across eight weeks, Shruti could identify two decisions that any of the three pages had changed.

The refill-rate disagreement was worse than embarrassing; it was material. Exhibit 2 sets out the three live definitions. Anand's version counted any customer who ordered again within sixty days. The operations version counted refills fulfilled against refill reminders sent. Ravi Menon, the data scientist in Toronto, had a third definition built on prescription-implied due dates — the closest thing to a clinically meaningful measure, and the one that produced the lowest number. The three were not variants of one metric; they answered three different questions, and the company had been using them interchangeably in board material for eighteen months.

Two further complications had surfaced. First, Ravi had shown that the most recent three days of any operations series were systematically understated, because third-party delivery scans arrived in nightly batches and some partners uploaded twice a week. Every Monday morning, therefore, the delivery-performance tile showed a dip that resolved itself by Wednesday, and the fulfilment team had learned to ignore Mondays — a habit that would be catastrophic during the Diwali fortnight, when Monday was exactly when a real dip would occur. Second, the DPDP rebuild meant that account-level views containing medicine names could be seen only by a restricted group; any company-wide dashboard would have to work at aggregate grain, which ruled out some of what the care team wanted.

4. The people

Vikram Raghavan, head of engineering, Pune. Vikram wanted funding for a data platform: a semantic layer where each metric was defined once, certified, and versioned, plus a migration of all three dashboards onto it. He estimated four engineers for two quarters — about ₹1.4 crore fully loaded — and argued, with some justice, that anything less would leave the definitions to fork again within a year. He was also aware that the same four engineers were the only ones who could deliver the ONDC integration that Suresh had promised the board for Q4.

Ishita Bose, product designer, Berlin. Ishita had reviewed all sixty-one tiles and concluded that the company's problem was not data but legibility. Her position was that a dashboard nobody can read in four seconds is not a data problem at any budget, and that one well-designed page on existing pipelines would change behaviour faster than a platform. The seven-and-a-half-hour time difference meant she joined Indian reviews at six in the morning her time, which gave her a sharp view of which meetings were worth attending.

Ravi Menon, data scientist, Toronto. Ravi wanted the definitions settled before anything was built, and had volunteered to write a one-line specification for each proposed tile — event, filter, grain, window, owner, decision rule. He was blunt that a page which launched with three ambiguous metrics would simply move the argument to a new venue. His working hours overlapped with Hyderabad only between 6:30 and 9:30 in the evening India time, which shaped how quickly definitional questions could be resolved.

Lalitha Krishnan, head of customer care, Singapore. Lalitha ran care for India and the Gulf, and her concern was exclusion. If the company page carried only orders, margin and delivery, care would remain invisible and under-resourced; her first-response time had drifted from 34 to 52 minutes over two quarters with no consequence. She also owned the Dubai client's monthly report and wanted its numbers to come off the same source as the company dashboard, so that she was not explaining discrepancies to a client at 9 p.m. Singapore time.

Exhibit 2 says that the single metric the strategy depends on has no definition of record, and that the most meaningful version is also the least precise — a trade-off Shruti will have to make explicitly rather than duck. 6. The options

Option A — fund the platform first. Approve Vikram's ₹1.4 crore and four engineers for two quarters. Every metric gets defined once, certified and versioned; the Dubai report and the company dashboard come off the same source; the refill-rate argument ends permanently. The cost is that nothing new is readable until January 2027, the company goes through Diwali on the sediment it already has, and the ONDC integration promised to the board slips or is staffed by hiring the company has not budgeted for.

Option B — ship nine tiles in two weeks. Build Exhibit 3 on existing pipelines, with Ravi writing a one-line specification for each tile and a single canonical definition declared for refill rate, conversion and active customer. Launch the Monday reading on 5 October with a twenty-five-minute timebox, a visible freshness banner and a greyed incomplete window on the 3PL tile. The cost is that the definitional mess underneath survives, two tiles will be provisional every Monday, the Dubai report continues to be produced separately, and Vikram will point out — correctly — that this is a patch.

Option C — federate. Keep the three dashboards, appoint a named owner for each contested metric, and hold one monthly reconciliation meeting where the numbers are squared. Nobody loses their instrument, no engineering is diverted, and care keeps its page. The cost is that it does not answer what Suresh asked for, cross-functional diagnosis stays impossible because no one page carries the whole identity, and the sixty-one tiles remain sixty-one tiles.

7. Questions for discussion

1. What, precisely, is the problem Suresh Nadkarni asked Shruti to solve — a data-infrastructure problem, a definitional problem, or a meeting problem? What evidence in Exhibits 1 and 2 supports your reading?

2. Ravi's refill-rate definition is the most meaningful and the least precise. On what grounds should a company choose a noisier metric that measures the right thing over a cleaner one that measures something adjacent?

3. Lalitha wants care metrics on the page and the Dubai report drawn from the same source. Which of her two requests should Shruti grant, and what does the answer reveal about the difference between a dashboard and a report?

4. It is Monday, 28 September. Shruti must circulate one design. Which option does she choose, what does she explicitly refuse, and what would she tell Vikram to make him an ally rather than an obstacle?

8. A note for the learner

This case is about the difference between having data and having an instrument. The topic lens — building a metrics dashboard — insists on four questions for every number: who reads it, at what cadence, who owns it, and what decision it changes. Exhibit 1 shows that Aushadhi Direct's sixty-one tiles fail all four for most of their surface area; two decisions in eight weeks across three pages is not a reporting shortfall, it is the absence of a reading ritual. That reframing matters, because a data platform cannot manufacture a ritual, and a ritual can be created in a fortnight.

A well-reasoned answer will do three things. It will separate the meeting problem from the plumbing problem and sequence them, rather than treating ₹1.4 crore as the price of clarity. It will insist on a definition of record before launch — not for all sixty-one metrics, but for the three that appear in board material — because a page launched with ambiguous definitions relocates the argument instead of ending it. And it will treat the freshness limitation as a design element to be published rather than a defect to be hidden: a greyed incomplete window with the lag stated is honest and usable; an unlabelled dip that everyone has learned to ignore is dangerous precisely when it stops being an artefact.

One defensible path is Option B with three amendments. Ship the nine tiles for 5 October, but (i) have Ravi publish the one-line specification for each tile in the same document, with refill rate declared canonically as the prescription-due-date version and the other two renamed — “60-day repeat rate” and “reminder response rate” — so that all three can continue to exist without contaminating each other; (ii) grant Lalitha her first request and refuse the second, putting care first-response time in the guardrail row because it is a weekly decision input, while declaring the Dubai monthly report a separate contractual deliverable with its own reconciliation, since a client report and an internal dashboard have different accuracy obligations; (iii) give Vikram a gate rather than a refusal — instrument the new page's own usage, and in January bring Suresh evidence of which tiles were actually read and which definitions broke, as the business case for the platform. If in six weeks the Monday reading has produced fewer than two decisions, the correct response is to retire the page, not to add tiles to it.

The reasoning behind that path is sequencing under a deadline. Diwali is six weeks away and represents the year's largest volume; the value of a readable page during that fortnight is high and perishable, while the value of a semantic layer is real but arrives after the peak has passed. Option A optimises for permanence at the cost of the one period where the company most needs to see clearly; Option C preserves peace at the cost of the closed arithmetic that makes cross-functional diagnosis possible at all. Option B is the only one that produces, before the peak, a page on which a fall in prescription verification from 93.1 to 87.3 per cent is visible to the same five people who can act on it.

Building a Metrics Dashboard

A dashboard is not a display. It is an inference instrument operating under two budgets — a signal-to-noise budget and a decision-latency budget — and almost every argument practitioners have about dashboards is really an argument about which of those two budgets binds.

1. Two rooms, one week apart

On Tuesday, 14 January 2025, Aditi Rangachari, Director of Product at Roshandaan Systems, sat with a printout of twelve weeks of a single number. Roshandaan sells field-service software to industrial maintenance firms — 1,240 paying accounts across India and Southeast Asia, average contract ₹11 lakh a year, renewals clustered at quarter ends. The number was the share of accounts completing at least one full work-order cycle in the week: schedule, dispatch, close, invoice. It had hovered near 46% all quarter. In the week of 16 December it dropped to 43.1%, and the leadership dashboard showed that tile red. The VP of Engineering pulled two people off the mobile roadmap for nine days to hunt for the cause. They found nothing. Aditi's problem was not the drop. It was that she could not tell anyone in the room, with a straight face, whether 43.1% had been a real event at all — and until she could, every red tile was going to cost engineering weeks she had not budgeted.

Eight days later and 340 kilometres away, Kabir Menon faced the mirror image. Kabir was Head of Product at Jharokha Labs, an AI-native company whose product read incoming customer-support email and proposed a reply for a human agent to accept, edit or reject: 61 enterprise clients, roughly 84,000 suggestions a week. Its headline tile was suggestion acceptance rate, the fraction of proposals an agent sent without material edit. In the week of 13 January it rose from 26.0% to 35.0% — a nine-point jump, far outside anything the tile had done before, and the CEO had already told two investors. Kabir spent the weekend segmenting. Acceptance had risen by exactly one percentage point in each of the two client segments that mattered; the entire nine-point headline move came from a change in which segment sent the volume. Worse, the model had been retrained on 9 January, so the numbers before and after were not measurements of the same thing.

Aditi had a metric too noisy to act on and a dashboard that did not say so. Kabir had a metric precise to a sixth of a point and a dashboard that did not know its own denominator had moved. Both had done everything the standard curriculum asks. Both dashboards were, strictly, working. Both were producing wrong decisions.

2. The idea, and the five schools that disagree about it

Define the object precisely. A metrics dashboard is a bounded set of quantities, each with a definition, an owner, a cadence and a pre-agreed decision rule, presented together so a group can detect a change worth acting on and allocate attention to it in one reading. Four words carry the load. Bounded: the cost of a tile is not the pixels it occupies but the attention it takes from every other tile, forever. Detect: the function is inferential — a hypothesis test conducted by eye. Pre-agreed: a decision rule invented after seeing the number is not a rule. Attention: that, not data, is the scarce resource the instrument allocates.

The practice has four ancestors, and most modern disagreements are inherited rather than discovered. In 1919 DuPont decomposed return on investment into margin × turnover × leverage, producing the first driver tree and the idea that a top-line number should be shown as the arithmetic of its parts. In 1924 Walter Shewhart, at Western Electric, drew the first control chart and made the claim most inconvenient for product managers: in any process most variation is routine, and treating routine variation as a signal makes the process worse. Deming carried it into management; Donald Wheeler restated it in Understanding Variation (1993). In 1992 Kaplan and Norton's Balanced Scorecard argued that a single financial measure is gameable and leading indicators must accompany lagging ones. From roughly 2003 Amazon's Weekly Business Review made the dashboard a ritual with a fixed agenda and a fixed owner per line, on the theory that the meeting, not the chart, is the artefact. The software-native layer arrived last: Croll and Yoskovitz's Lean Analytics (2013) and its One Metric That Matters, the North Star metric, and Google's SRE discipline of service-level objectives and error budgets (2016), which held that humans reading charts on a schedule is itself a failure mode.

Those ancestors produce five live schools. The single-number school signs: one metric should dominate organisational attention at any moment, and the dashboard's job is to protect its primacy; it will not sign that a balanced set of eight is more rigorous. The decomposition school signs: a dashboard must display an arithmetic identity, so movement can be attributed to a named lever with a named owner; it will not sign that one number suffices, because one number cannot be attributed. The scorecard school signs: every growth tile needs a paired counter-metric, or the dashboard becomes an engine for Goodhart's law; it will not sign that the page should be optimised for the fastest read. The process-control school signs: a point estimate with a red/green threshold is not a decision rule; it will not sign that team judgement substitutes for knowing the standard error. The observability school signs: anything that must be caught within hours should page a machine-defined owner automatically; it will not sign that weekly reading is where detection happens.

Aditi's problem sits in the gap between the decomposition school, which built her dashboard, and the process-control school, which was never consulted. Kabir's adds an AI-native complication none of the five anticipated: a metric whose measuring instrument is retrained while the measurement is in progress.

3. Mechanics: the two budgets, worked through

The signal budget

Expert practice adds two calculations to the standard build sequence, both usually left implicit: what movement in a tile is distinguishable from noise, and how long the dashboard takes to say anything. Start with Aditi's tile: a proportion over 1,240 accounts, about 46% of which complete a full work-order cycle in a week. Treating account behaviour as independent week to week, the standard error is √(p(1−p)/n) = √(0.46 × 0.54 / 1240) = 0.0142, or 1.42 percentage points. A ±2σ band is therefore roughly ±2.8 points: anything between 43.2% and 48.8% is what this metric does when nothing is happening. The 43.1% that cost nine engineer-days sits a tenth of a point outside that band — the weakest possible alarm, and exactly the kind a red/green threshold cannot tell from a real one.

Figure 1. The nine engineer-days Roshandaan spent chasing the December drop bought a move one-tenth of a point outside its own routine band. The band is the difference between a dashboard that allocates attention and one that consumes it.

The same arithmetic tells Aditi what her dashboard can and cannot do. To detect an effect of size d at ±2σ she needs enough weeks that the pooled standard error, σ/√k, falls below d/2 — that is, k ≥ (2σ/d)². For three points, k ≥ (2 × 1.42 / 3)² = 0.90: one week. For two points, k ≥ 2.02: three weeks. For one point, k ≥ 8.1: nine weeks. Roshandaan's board cares about one-point moves, because a point is worth roughly ₹1.4 crore of renewal risk across the base. Her weekly dashboard cannot see one point; it can see three, and three is already a crisis. Pooling to a monthly cadence, k = 4, brings the detectable effect to 1.42 points. The right response to a noisy tile is almost never to stare at it harder; it is to change the window, the denominator, or the metric.

Kabir's tile has the opposite profile. At 84,000 suggestions a week and p = 0.31, σ = √(0.31 × 0.69 / 84000) = 0.0016 — 0.16 percentage points, a ±2σ band of ±0.32. He can detect a third of a point in a single week. That is not an unambiguous advantage: a band that tight flags something almost every week, and a dashboard that is always red is indistinguishable from one that is always green.

The multiple-comparison tax

The second-order effect beginners never see is that tiles interact statistically. A ±2σ band carries a per-tile false-alarm probability of about 4.6% in any week; tiles are not independent, but treating them as such gives an upper bound of tile count × 0.046 chance alarms per week.

Read the third column. A twenty-two-tile dashboard read at ±2σ produces, on average, one red tile every week for no reason whatsoever. That is not a metaphor about clutter; it is the mechanism by which large dashboards destroy their own credibility. The team learns, correctly, that red means nothing, and then fails to react the week it means something. Widening to ±3σ buys that credibility back — one chance alarm every seventeen weeks — at the price of power: a ±3σ rule needs k ≥ (3σ/d)², twenty weeks rather than nine for Aditi's one-point effect. No setting of the dial is free. The only lever that improves both terms at once is cutting tiles, which is why a small committed set is a statistical argument and not an aesthetic one.

The latency budget

The second calculation converts delay into rupees. Expected detection lag is roughly (cadence ÷ 2) + (weeks of pooling required), and the design's cost is that lag times the weekly cost of the undetected condition. For Aditi's one-point drop — about 9.5 weeks — against ₹1.4 crore of annual renewal risk, roughly ₹2.7 lakh a week, that is ₹26 lakh per undetected episode. A monthly pooled view with a formal band cuts pooling to four weeks and lag to about six, saving ₹9 lakh per episode while reducing how often anyone looks. That inversion — read it less often, learn more from it — most reliably separates practitioners who have done this arithmetic from those who have not.

4. The conditions, stated as testable claims

Five conditions determine whether a weekly dashboard tile earns its place. Each is a claim that can be checked before the tile is built, and each fails for at least one of our two protagonists.

C3 is where the idea becomes actively misleading rather than merely weak. A tile is an implicit claim that this week's number and last week's measure the same quantity. When the denominator is itself a decision variable, that claim is false and the dashboard will confidently report the opposite of what happened. Kabir's rise is the canonical form. In the week of 6 January, 20,000 suggestions came from short-form tickets at 38% acceptance and 60,000 from long-form at 22% — blended, 26.0%. In the week of 13 January a large client moved its long-form queue elsewhere, inverting the mix: 60,000 short-form at 39%, 20,000 long-form at 23%, blended 35.0%. Both segments improved by one point; the headline improved by nine. Simpson's paradox is not a curiosity here. It is the default behaviour of any ratio tile whose denominator composition is not pinned, and the reason experts insist a ratio tile display its numerator and denominator beside it.

5. Hard edges: where the clean model stops working

The five conditions assume a single product, a single population and a single owner. Real dashboards break at the seams where those assumptions fail.

Multi-product and hardware. Gavaksh Instruments sells connected cold-chain monitors to pharmaceutical distributors: 14,200 devices plus a software console. Its group dashboard summed engagement across three lines, so a collapse in one could be masked by growth in another for a full quarter. The mature answer is a template, not a smarter aggregate — the same six tiles, identically defined, once per line, plus one portfolio page whose tiles are deliberately different (capital allocation, gross margin by line, fleet failure rate), because portfolio decisions are not product decisions. Hardware adds a metric class software teams rarely meet: one whose population ages. Monitors installed in 2022 fail at a different rate from the 2024 cohort, so a blended failure rate drifts purely from installed-base composition. The remedy is vintage-stratified tiles — Simpson's paradox in different clothing.

Two-sided. Khidki Bazaar, a marketplace for surplus industrial spares, learned that supply-side and demand-side dashboards can both look healthy while the market dies. Its rescuing tile belonged to neither side: fill rate, the share of buyer requests matched within 48 hours. Cross-side tiles have a structural ownership problem — nobody on either side controls them — and the honest resolution is a two-owner tile with a standing rule about who speaks first.

Regulated. Deedbaan Payments, a licensed payment aggregator, cannot show merchant-level transaction data to its whole leadership team under its own access policy. The consequence is a tiered dashboard, and the failure mode is subtle: the version reaching the executive room is the one with the constrained tiles removed, so the blind spot sits exactly where regulatory risk is highest. Mature regulated firms answer with aggregated proxies designed to be shareable — a count of merchants breaching a threshold rather than the breaches themselves.

AI-native. Jharokha's deeper problem is non-stationarity by design: every retrain changes the instrument. Serious AI teams run two parallel measurements — the live tile, which moves with traffic mix and model version, and a frozen held-out evaluation set of several thousand labelled cases re-scored after each retrain, which moves only with model quality. When the two diverge, the divergence is the finding.

The organisational seam. What mature companies say they do is assign one owner per tile. What they actually do, and what makes the ritual work, is hold a thirty-minute pre-read in which owners agree the narrative beforehand — usually described as inefficiency. It is not. The dashboard's real function in a large organisation is to force weekly preparation; the meeting is where prepared explanations are challenged, not where discovery happens. A dashboard that produces genuine surprise every week is one whose owners are not reading it.

6. Nine distinctions that separate expert from competent

The output is attention, not information. The tell: an expert asked to add a tile asks which tile comes off. The obvious reading — that an extra chart is nearly free because nobody has to look at it — is wrong twice: it raises the chance-alarm rate for every other tile, and a page that cannot be read in four minutes stops being read at all.

Experts read ranges, not points. The tell: before agreeing a threshold they ask for the metric's historical week-to-week standard deviation. The obvious reading is that thresholds follow business importance — "alert me below 45%" — which confuses what matters with what is detectable, and sets a line Aditi's metric crosses by chance one week in four.

Ratios conceal the lever. The tell: an expert asks for numerator and denominator beside the percentage. The obvious reading — that a rate is the normalised and therefore superior form — fails whenever the denominator is something the company controls. Kabir's nine points came entirely from a denominator he could have watched.

Cadence is set by the slower of two clocks. The tell: an expert asks when the team could next actually change this number. The obvious reading is that faster reading is more responsive. If the lever moves quarterly, a weekly tile yields twelve readings of which eleven can produce no action — and those eleven train the team to skim.

The owner is whoever can move the number, not whoever can explain it. The tell: an expert watches who speaks when a tile goes red. If the analyst answers, ownership is fictional — an analyst can describe a movement, not cause a different one. The obvious reading, that whoever is closest to the data should own the tile, gets it backwards.

Every growth tile needs a paired guardrail. The tell: an expert reads the page for what is missing, asking what would happen if each tile were optimised ruthlessly. Kabir's acceptance rate reaches 90% by suppressing every uncertain suggestion — improving the tile while halving the product's value. The guardrail is coverage: suggestions offered per ticket, always shown beside acceptance.

Definitions decay silently. The tell: an expert asks when the query behind a tile last changed and who approved it. The obvious reading is that a tile is as trustworthy as its pipeline; it is as trustworthy as its least-documented definition change. A tile whose SQL was quietly edited eleven weeks ago has eleven weeks of history not comparable to today.

Pipeline health is itself a tile. The tell: an expert checks the freshness stamp and row count before reading any number. The obvious reading is that missing data appears as a visible gap. It usually appears as a plausible decline, which is far more expensive, because a plausible decline gets investigated by product managers rather than data engineers.

The value is in the argument, not the page. The tell: an expert judges a dashboard by watching the meeting and counting the minutes spent on the tiles that moved. The obvious reading is that a good dashboard makes the meeting shorter. It makes it narrower — same length, one subject, an actual disagreement resolved.

7. What changes by product type and stage

Three differences are real and one is imagined. Sample size sets everything downstream: a consumer product with millions of weekly events can run tight bands and weekly cadence honestly, a B2B product with 1,240 accounts cannot, and an enterprise product with 40 accounts should abandon proportions for named-account tracking, because at n = 40 the standard error on a 46% rate is 7.9 points and no weekly reading means anything. Non-stationarity is mild in mature consumer products, severe in marketplaces where liquidity feeds back on itself, structural in AI products. Ownership topology differs: in consumer products one team usually controls the lever; in marketplaces and platforms none does, so tiles need co-owners; in hardware the lever may sit in manufacturing, months upstream of anything a PM can change this quarter.

The imagined difference is that product types need different frameworks. They do not. Breadth, frequency and depth decompose enterprise seat usage as cleanly as grocery orders; only units and windows change. The mistake is importing the consumer cadence with the consumer decomposition.

Stage changes the failure mode more than the design. A seed-stage dashboard fails by going stale — nobody updates the spreadsheet during a crunch. A Series-B dashboard fails by sprawl, one tile per stakeholder question, which is where Roshandaan was. A late-stage dashboard fails by definitional divergence: two teams computing "active account" two ways, each correct within its own query — a governance problem requiring a semantic layer and a metric registry, not a better chart.

8. Three worked examples

Gavaksh Instruments: vintage stratification

Gavaksh's fleet failure tile read 2.4% of devices reporting a fault per month, stable for five quarters, never discussed. Stratifying by installation vintage in March 2025 showed the 2022 cohort at 5.1% and the 2024 cohort at 0.9%, the newer cohort growing fast enough to hold the blend flat. The blended tile was mathematically correct and operationally useless: an ageing problem worth ₹3.8 crore in warranty exposure had been invisible for fifteen months. The fix cost one afternoon — three tiles instead of one — and changed the replacement-parts forecast at once.

Khidki Bazaar: the cross-side tile nobody owned

Through the second half of 2024 Khidki's supply dashboard showed listings up 30% and its demand dashboard showed buyer signups up 24%. Fill rate, on neither page, had fallen from 71% to 61%. Added in January 2025 with two named owners, it yielded a diagnosis in four days: listings were growing in categories where demand was not. Khidki reallocated ₹1.2 crore of supply-acquisition spend and fill rate recovered to 69% in eleven weeks. The lesson is not that fill rate is a good metric; it is that the tiles most worth having are the ones no team will volunteer to own.

Deedbaan Payments: the failure, and the recovery

Deedbaan did everything the literature recommends, and too much of it. In 2024 it consolidated forty tiles into a governed BI dashboard with automated threshold alerts on every one — a "single source of truth" its CTO called the end of metric arguments. At ±2σ across forty tiles the page produced roughly two chance alarms a week and the alerting layer escalated all of them; within four months the operations team had a filter rule sending alerts to a folder nobody read. On 3 July 2024 settlement-failure rate for one acquiring bank rose from 0.4% to 2.1% and stayed there nine days before a merchant complaint surfaced it — ₹2.1 crore in failed transaction value and a regulatory disclosure.

The recovery inverted the obvious remedy. Deedbaan did not tune the thresholds. It split the artefact: five committed tiles at ±3σ read by humans on a Monday, and a separate machine-owned layer of four service-level objectives with error budgets that page an on-call engineer within minutes and never appear in the weekly meeting. The remaining thirty-one tiles became an on-demand diagnostic library, explicitly not read on a cadence. Alarms in the weekly review fell from two a week to one every four months; mean time to detect a settlement anomaly fell from nine days to under an hour. The dashboard got smaller and slower; the organisation got faster. That is the pattern.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Each of the following has a characteristic early sign that appears well before the cost lands, and a single question that catches it.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether control limits belong on a product dashboard. The process-control position, in its strongest form: routine variation is the majority of what any dashboard displays, reacting to it is what Deming called tampering, and tampering demonstrably increases variance. The evidence is a century of manufacturing practice and the arithmetic above. The counter-position is not innumeracy: control charts assume a stable process, and product development is a deliberate, continuous attempt to shift it — every launch invalidates the historical band used to judge it, so limits estimated from the last twelve weeks are systematically wrong in exactly the weeks that matter most. For the SPC position to be wrong, product metrics would have to be non-stationary enough that historical bands carry no information; for the counter-position to be wrong, launch effects would have to be rare enough that most weeks are genuinely in-control. Both are empirical claims about a specific product, and neither side has generalisable data.

One number or a small set. The single-metric position rests on organisational attention: focus is scarce, and a team that agrees on one number moves faster than one negotiating among eight. The evidence is anecdotal but consistent across growth practice. The scorecard position rests on Goodhart's law, closer to a theorem than an observation: any single optimised measure eventually stops measuring what it proxied. Each steelman concedes something — focus advocates accept guardrails they decline to call metrics, scorecard advocates accept that one metric leads. The genuine disagreement is how many guardrails a team can hold in mind, and nobody has measured it.

Ritual or automation. The observability position holds that anything requiring detection within hours must be machine-detected, that humans reading weekly charts admits missing instrumentation, and that Deedbaan's recovery proves it. The ritual position holds that weekly reading exists to produce shared interpretation and accountability, not detection — the meeting is where an organisation decides what a number means, which no alert can do. Deedbaan's split is one synthesis, but it is not free: it requires two measurement systems under two governance models, and smaller companies attempting it usually maintain neither properly.

A fourth disagreement is quieter: whether leadership should read the same page as the teams. Shared pages create alignment and also the pressure that makes teams stop reporting honestly, and those who choose transparency pay in gaming they rarely measure.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this builds a good dashboard. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways. They negotiate the decision before the metric: the first question is never "what should we measure" but "what will we do differently, and when is the soonest we could do it." They treat tile count as a fixed budget with a queue, so adding a tile is a trade argued in the same meeting, not a favour granted. They ask for variance before value, which sounds pedantic until it saves nine engineer-days a quarter. And they read their own dashboards adversarially — hunting the tile that has not moved in eleven weeks, the ratio whose denominator is a decision, the owner never once asked a hard question — because a dashboard's characteristic failure is not being wrong but being politely ignored while everyone continues to believe it works.

12. What each of them decided

Aditi Rangachari kept the completion-rate tile but changed what it was: a ±2σ band on a trailing twenty-six weeks, a four-week pooled reading with weekly points shown as context rather than alarms, and the band width printed in the tile caption so nobody could set a threshold without confronting it. She cut Roshandaan's page from twenty-two tiles to seven, moving the rest into a diagnostic library available on request. Her reasoning was economic, not statistical: at twenty-two tiles the page generated about one false alarm a week, each costing two to nine engineering days — roughly ₹40 lakh a year of capacity spent on nothing. She told her CEO the dashboard would now catch less, later, and cost less, and that the December incident would not have been flagged at all, which was the correct outcome.

Kabir Menon did not cut tiles. He split acceptance rate into three — short-form, long-form, and a volume-mix indicator showing the share of each — and added a coverage guardrail beside them. He then built the frozen evaluation set: 4,000 labelled tickets re-scored after every retrain, reported as a separate tile stamped with the model version, so model quality and traffic mix could never again be confused. His constraint was never resolution; it was that a precise number about a shifting population is more dangerous than an imprecise one, because it invites confidence. He also told his CEO to retract the nine-point claim — the most expensive two sentences of his year, and the cheapest thing he did all quarter.

For discussion.

  1. Aditi's redesigned dashboard would not have flagged the December drop. Is a measurement system that misses real events by design defensible to a board, and what would you show them to defend it?
  2. Kabir's frozen evaluation set measures model quality honestly but has no link to revenue; his live tile connects to revenue but cannot be trusted week to week. Which belongs on the leadership page, and what does that imply about what such pages are for?
  3. Deedbaan's recovery required two measurement systems under different governance. At what company size does that stop being affordable, and what should a fifty-person company do instead?

13. Going deeper

Breadth × depth × frequency
Gives a dashboard its attributable structure; each lever carries its own sample size, so it is where the variance arithmetic applies.
Instrumentation with product analytics tools
Decides which tiles are possible and how far they can be trusted; definitional divergence and denominator drift originate here.
Release criteria and success metrics
Applies the resolution question at launch level: which tile a release may move, by how much, and whether that is detectable.
Designing dashboards people read
The layout, hierarchy and ritual that decide whether a sound page is actually consumed — the human half of this argument.
What makes a good metric
The per-tile admission test — sensitivity, specificity, gameability — deciding what survives a tile budget.
Vanity vs actionable metrics
The cheapest way to cut tile count, and so the chance-alarm rate in Table 1.
GAME framework
Binds goal, action, metric and evaluation into one statement, so no tile exists without a pre-agreed decision rule.
Acquisition, retention, monetisation actions
Maps each tile to the intervention class that can move it — how Figure 3's action clock gets its values.
Direct vs proxy, magnitude vs ratio
The formal treatment of the ratio problem behind Kabir's week, and when a proxy is worth its measurement error.
North Star metric
The single-number school's strongest artefact; its limits make Section 10's disagreement legible rather than tribal.

Building a Metrics Dashboard

1. A Monday morning in Bengaluru

On the second Monday of March 2025, Rhea Sundaram, VP of Product at Qiladar Mart, a fifteen-minute grocery delivery company operating out of Bengaluru, Pune and Hyderabad, opened the company's leadership dashboard forty minutes before the weekly review and counted the tiles. There were twenty-two of them: gross merchandise value, app downloads, registered users, average session length, cart abandonment, push notification opt-in rate, sixteen more. The dashboard had grown the way most dashboards grow — one tile at a time, each added because someone on the leadership team asked a question in a meeting eight months ago and an analyst obliged. No one had ever removed one.

Qiladar Mart had just closed a ₹140 crore Series C, and its board had asked for a standing weekly metrics review, chaired by Rhea, starting that Friday. The investors did not want a data dump; they wanted to know whether the team could tell, week over week, if the business was getting healthier or sicker, and whether the product organisation would act on what it saw. Rhea had eleven days to turn a sprawling reporting habit into something a seven-person leadership team could actually read, argue about, and use to decide what to build next quarter. The stakes were not abstract: Qiladar's dark-store network was burning roughly ₹3.1 crore a month, and the board had been explicit that the next funding conversation would turn on whether growth was coming from genuine repeat behaviour or from discount-driven trial that would evaporate the moment the coupons stopped.

2. The idea, precisely stated

A metrics dashboard, in the sense this page means, is a small, fixed set of numbers, each with a named owner, a defined cadence, and an explicit decision it is meant to inform, presented together so a team can read it in one sitting and act on what has changed. It is not a report — a report is written after the fact to explain what happened. A dashboard is read before a decision, on a schedule, by people who have agreed in advance what they will do if a number moves.

The practice traces to two older disciplines that met inside product organisations in the 2010s: the operating-review culture of manufacturing and retail, where a small number of KPIs (on-time delivery, inventory turns, gross margin) were reviewed weekly by plant managers long before software existed to automate it, and the instrumentation discipline that grew out of web analytics — first through tools such as Google Analytics and Mixpanel in the late 2000s, later formalised by writers like Alistair Croll and Benjamin Yoskovitz in Lean Analytics (2013), who argued that every stage of a company needs exactly one metric that matters most right now, not a wall of charts. Product organisations folded both traditions into the discipline now taught alongside metrics trees: decompose the outcome into its drivers, instrument the events that feed those drivers, and build a dashboard that shows the decomposition on a cadence tight enough to catch problems while they are still cheap to fix.

The sentence Rhea could say in the boardroom without sounding glib: "A dashboard earns its place on this table only if a specific person reads it every week and it changes what we build next."

3. How it actually works

Building a working dashboard is not a design exercise; it is a sequence of decisions, most of which practitioners skip because they feel obvious until the dashboard is live and nobody trusts it.

Step one — pick the decomposition, not the metric. Rhea did not start with "what should be on the dashboard." She started with the metrics tree the product team had already built the month before: Weekly Active Ordering Households (the outcome) decomposed into Breadth (the share of registered households in a serviceable pincode who order at least once in the week), Frequency (average orders per ordering household that week), and Depth (average order value). This breadth × frequency × depth structure is the same decomposition used for any engagement outcome — it separates "are we reaching people," "are they coming back," and "are they spending more" into three levers that respond to different interventions, so a single blended number never has to carry all three questions at once.

Step two — confirm the events actually exist and are trustworthy. A dashboard can only show what has been instrumented. Rhea's team checked that every event feeding the three levers — app_open, order_placed, order_value, household_pincode_mapped — was firing reliably, deduplicated, and timestamped in the warehouse, not just logged client-side. One event failed this check: order_value was being logged before coupon deduction on Android but after deduction on iOS, silently inflating Depth by roughly 6% on one platform. This is the step most teams skip, and it is the single most common reason a dashboard, once launched, is quietly ignored within six weeks — people stop trusting numbers that visibly disagree with what they know from the ground.

Step three — assign one owner and one decision per tile. Every number on the dashboard got a name next to it — not a team, a person — and a one-line answer to "what do we do differently if this moves 15% in either direction." Breadth was owned by the growth lead, Frequency by Rhea herself, Depth by the merchandising lead. A tile with no answer to that question was cut, regardless of how interesting it was.

Step four — set the cadence to match the decision cycle, and build the freshness signal in. Weekly was right for Qiladar because dark-store staffing and promotional spend could actually be adjusted week to week; a metric that only mattered on a monthly cycle (cohort retention at day 90, say) was demoted to a monthly appendix rather than cluttering the weekly page. Each tile also carried a small "data as of" timestamp, because a dashboard that cannot tell you how stale it is will eventually mislead someone at the worst possible moment.

Figure 1. The breadth × frequency × depth decomposition Rhea's dashboard was built around, with the owner named against each lever — the discipline that turns a metrics tree into something a person is accountable for.

4. The arithmetic, worked through twice

Take the HSR Layout pincode cluster, one of eleven Qiladar serves in Bengaluru. It has 42,000 registered households. In the week of 3–9 March 2025, Breadth was 18%, meaning 7,560 households placed at least one order. Frequency among those ordering households was 1.4 orders per week, giving 10,584 orders for the cluster. Depth — average order value — was ₹560. Weekly revenue for the cluster is Breadth-derived orders multiplied by Depth: 10,584 orders × ₹560 = ₹59,27,040, or roughly ₹59.3 lakh.

Now change one input and hold the other two constant, which is exactly the exercise a dashboard is supposed to make easy. Suppose a Holi promotional week lifts Frequency from 1.4 to 1.6 orders per ordering household — people who were already ordering simply order more often — while Breadth (18%) and Depth (₹560) stay flat. Orders become 7,560 × 1.6 = 12,096, and revenue becomes 12,096 × ₹560 = ₹67,73,760, about ₹67.7 lakh — a 14.3% lift from a single lever moving. Compare that with the same 14.3% target pursued by moving Breadth instead, from 18% to 20.6%: ordering households rise to 8,652, orders to 12,113 at the same 1.4 frequency, revenue to roughly ₹67.8 lakh. Arithmetically the two paths land in nearly the same place, but operationally they are entirely different projects — one is a retention and habit-formation problem aimed at existing customers, the other is an acquisition and coverage problem aimed at households Qiladar has never converted. A dashboard that only shows the blended revenue number cannot tell a reader which of these two very different projects is actually working; a dashboard that shows the three levers separately can, in five seconds, tell Rhea which lever moved and therefore which team gets credit and which intervention to repeat.

5. What a learner must notice

A decomposition is not an explanation

Breadth × Frequency × Depth tells Rhea where a change in revenue came from; it does not tell her why Frequency rose. The dashboard is a symptom-locator, not a diagnosis. The moment a tile moves, the real work — talking to customers, checking a cohort, reading support tickets — begins rather than ends.

A dashboard is not the same artifact as a metrics tree

The tree is a static map of how metrics relate to one another, built once and revisited quarterly. The dashboard is the live, cadenced instrument built on top of that map. Teams that treat the two as interchangeable end up either rebuilding the tree every week (exhausting) or never updating the dashboard as strategy shifts (stale).

Instrumented is not the same as trustworthy

Qiladar's Android/iOS discrepancy in order_value shows why: an event can fire perfectly and still measure the wrong thing. Every dashboard needs a visible data-quality signal — a freshness timestamp at minimum, ideally a known-issues note — or it will eventually mislead someone with total confidence.

Weekly is a choice, not a default

Cadence should match how fast the underlying lever can actually be moved and how fast leadership can act on what it sees. Forcing a metric that only shifts meaningfully over ninety days onto a weekly tile manufactures noise that looks like signal.

Ownership means a name, not a function

"Growth owns Breadth" is not ownership; "Priya owns Breadth" is. The distinction matters the first time a number goes red and someone has to be in the room to explain it.

A metric earns its place only if an action follows

The test Rhea used — "what do we do differently if this moves 15%" — is the cleanest filter against vanity metrics. Total app downloads failed this test for Qiladar: a spike in downloads changed nothing about what the team would build next week, so it was cut from the weekly page and kept in a monthly appendix instead.

A dashboard cannot substitute for a hypothesis

Even a well-built dashboard only shows what has already happened. It cannot tell Rhea what Qiladar should try next; that still requires someone to propose an explanation and a test. The dashboard's job is to make it cheap to notice when that test worked.

More tiles is not more rigour

The instinct to add a tile every time a stakeholder asks a question is how dashboards balloon to twenty-two entries that nobody reads end to end. Rigour is choosing which six matter, not accumulating every number anyone has ever requested.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and stage

In a high-frequency consumer product like Qiladar Mart, breadth × frequency × depth maps cleanly onto weekly behaviour, and the dashboard's natural owner is Product or Growth. In a B2B SaaS business, the equivalent decomposition usually runs at the account level — breadth becomes the share of seats or accounts active, frequency becomes logins or key-workflow completions per account, depth becomes feature adoption within an account — and because enterprise usage moves more slowly, a genuinely weekly cadence is often too fast to show real signal; many B2B teams run the discipline monthly and let Customer Success, not Product, own the dashboard, since account health decisions sit there. A marketplace complicates the picture because it has two sides that can diverge: Qiladar's dark-store partners and its ordering households need separate dashboards, plus a small set of cross-side metrics — fill rate, match rate, time-to-fulfilment — that neither side's dashboard alone would surface.

Stage changes the dashboard's machinery more than its logic. An early-stage team, as Qiladar effectively still was, can run a dashboard as a shared spreadsheet updated by hand each Friday, judgment exercised case by case. A later-stage company needs the same tiles automated through a BI layer — Qiladar was already migrating from spreadsheets to Looker — with metric definitions frozen in a semantic layer so "order_value" means exactly one thing no matter who queries it, because at scale two teams quietly computing the same metric two different ways is a governance failure, not a minor embarrassment.

7. Where dashboards go wrong

The vanity parade. Symptom: a tile that always trends up and is never discussed in the room. Underlying misunderstanding: conflating growth with health. Cheapest diagnostic: ask what decision changes if the number moves 20% in either direction; silence means cut it.

Dashboard sprawl. Symptom: the weekly review spends its first twenty minutes scrolling before anyone says anything substantive. Underlying misunderstanding: that more data signals more rigour. Cheapest diagnostic: look back at the last five reviews and count how many tiles were ever the reason a decision changed.

The unowned metric. Symptom: a number drifts for three weeks with no one able to explain it in the meeting. Underlying misunderstanding: that a dashboard is self-explanatory once built. Cheapest diagnostic: ask, out loud, whose job it is if this tile turns red — if the room hesitates, there is no real owner.

The frozen dashboard. Symptom: the same charts have been on the page for eighteen months even though the company's strategy changed twice in that period. Underlying misunderstanding: treating the dashboard as a finished artifact rather than a living process. Cheapest diagnostic: check when a tile was last added or removed — if the answer is "never," the dashboard has stopped being read critically.

8. What good looks like

A sister portfolio company under the same investor, Kotwali Fresh, ran the same review the following quarter with six tiles on a single screen: Weekly Ordering Households, and Breadth, Frequency and Depth beneath it, plus fulfilment SLA and a data-freshness badge showing the hour the numbers were last refreshed. Each tile carried one owner's name and, in a small grey caption beneath it, the decision it existed to inform — "Frequency below 1.3 triggers a re-engagement push, owner: Lifecycle." The Monday review lasted twenty minutes: five to read, fifteen to argue about the one or two tiles that had actually moved. Nothing on the page had been added in the past nine months without something else being removed to make room. The board came away each week knowing not just what had happened, but who would do something about it and by when.

Figure 2. The weekly loop a working dashboard sits inside. A dashboard that stops at "Decide" without a visible "Act" step is a report with extra steps.

9. What Rhea decided

By the Thursday before the board's first weekly review, Rhea had cut the dashboard from twenty-two tiles to six: Weekly Ordering Households at the top, Breadth, Frequency and Depth beneath it with Priya, Rhea and the merchandising lead named against each, fulfilment SLA, and a data-freshness badge. She fixed the Android order_value bug before the numbers went live rather than footnoting it, because a footnoted known error is still an error a board will eventually catch and stop trusting the whole page over. She moved app downloads and eleven other tiles into a monthly appendix nobody was required to read in the weekly meeting. The first Friday review ran twenty-two minutes; the board spent most of it on why Frequency had slipped in the Hyderabad cluster, which was exactly the kind of question a six-tile dashboard was built to provoke and a twenty-two-tile one had spent eight months burying.

What Rhea would study next, and why, is designing dashboards people actually read rather than merely glance at — the layout, hierarchy and meeting ritual that determine whether a well-built dashboard survives contact with a busy leadership team's attention — together with release criteria and success metrics, which is the discipline of deciding, before a feature ships, which of these same tiles it is allowed to move and by how much before anyone calls it a success. Two questions worth sitting with: if a tile on your own team's dashboard moved 20% next week, could you name, right now, who would act on it and what they would do — and how many of your current tiles have gone unchanged, unquestioned, and unread for the last three months?

Nirikshan: The Dashboard Nobody Opened on Tuesday

Pune, Sunday 19 July 2026, 11.15 p.m. The rain has not stopped since Thursday. Aparna Deshmukh has one engineering squad for the September quarter, three numbers for the same thing, and a leadership meeting at nine that expects her to say which of them the company will be run on.

1. The night before

Aparna Deshmukh had moved her laptop twice to get away from the sound of water hitting the balcony of the flat in Aundh, and had settled at the dining table with two printouts and a mug of tea that had gone cold an hour ago. She was forty-three, had been Nirikshan's Vice-President of Product for three years and three months, and had spent the weekend on a single slide titled The Weekly Operating Review, FY27.

The slide was supposed to be easy. Nirikshan's leadership had asked for it in March, after a quarter in which two renewals had been lost that nobody had seen coming. Girish Patwardhan, the chief executive, had said the words that everyone had repeated since: we are a company of four hundred people flying on the CFO's spreadsheet and Nikhil's gut. The instruction had been simple — build one dashboard, put it in front of the leadership team every Tuesday morning, and make it the basis of the FY27 plan.

Four months later Aparna had a dashboard. It had fourteen tiles on it. She had, that afternoon, pulled its own usage logs, and Exhibit 1 was the printout in front of her: in the thirteen Tuesdays since it had gone live, the dashboard had been opened by a member of the leadership team on six of them, and by more than two members on two of them. In the same thirteen weeks, Sarita Iyengar's finance pack, a PDF of nine pages emailed at 7.30 a.m. on Monday, had been opened by everyone every week.

The second printout was Exhibit 3. It showed three counts of the same quantity — how many technicians actually used Nirikshan in the month of June — that differed from each other by 41 percent at the extremes. On Monday, Sarita intended to propose that FY27 pricing move from licensed seats to active technicians. Aparna could not tell her which of the three numbers to price on, and had not yet decided whether to say so in the room or beforehand.

Underneath both problems was the one that would be decided on Monday whether or not anybody framed it: Tanmay Bose had one squad free from 1 September, and there were two things it could build.

2. How Nirikshan got here

Nirikshan was founded in Pune in 2017 by Girish Patwardhan, who had spent eleven years at an industrial automation firm, and by two engineers from the College of Engineering Pune. The observation was ordinary and correct: that a large Indian plant ran on paper. Shift checklists, lockout-tagout registers, lubrication rounds, boiler logs, Factories Act statutory inspection records, vendor gate passes — all of it written by hand on printed forms, filed in steel almirahs, and reconstructed frantically whenever the Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health asked a question.

Nirikshan's product was an offline-first Android app for technicians and supervisors, and a web console for plant heads and corporate EHS teams. A technician walked a round with a phone, scanned a QR tag on an asset, filled a checklist, photographed a defect, and raised a work order. The phone might be in a basement, a cold store, or a captive power plant with no signal; the app queued everything and synced when it could. By June 2026 Nirikshan had 212 enterprise customers across cement, auto components, pharma, food processing, utilities and facilities management, roughly 94,000 licensed technician seats, and annual recurring revenue of ₹196 crore, of which 31 percent came from outside India.

The decision that constrains everything in this case was taken in November 2023. Nirikshan was competing for its largest deal to date — a fourteen-plant rollout for a diversified manufacturing group — against an established global asset-management suite carried by a large systems integrator. The customer's information security team made two demands: a single-tenant deployment inside the customer's own cloud tenancy, and a contractual undertaking that Nirikshan would collect no product telemetry of any kind from the deployment. Girish signed both. The deal closed at ₹11 crore a year and opened a category: by June 2026, Nirikshan had nineteen such single-tenant deployments, together worth ₹66 crore of ARR, or 34 percent of the company's revenue, from which the product organisation receives no usage data at all. Every dashboard Nirikshan has ever built describes the other 66 percent and labels it "the customer base".

3. The industry around it

Nirikshan's market in 2026 had three shapes of competitor. At the top sat the global enterprise asset management suites — SAP's and IBM Maximo among them — sold to Indian conglomerates by Infosys, TCS and Wipro as part of larger transformation programmes, expensive, complete, and slow to deploy. In the middle sat the Indian B2B SaaS cohort that Nirikshan was measured against by its investors: Freshworks, Zoho and Postman were the reference points quoted in every board deck, none of them competitors, all of them benchmarks for net revenue retention and for the discipline of running a product organisation on data. At the bottom sat a long tail of regional maintenance-software vendors and, far more dangerously, Excel.

Several forces bore on the decision. Indian manufacturing capital expenditure had run strong through the production-linked incentive schemes, and greenfield plants were the company's best-converting segment because they had no paper habit to unlearn. Statutory compliance was tightening: state factory inspectorates had moved to digital returns, and customers increasingly wanted their Nirikshan records to be the record of authority, which raised the stakes on data integrity and made customers nervous about anything that looked like the vendor reading their operational data. The DPDP Act's obligations sharpened this: technician names, photographs and location traces were personal data, and three of Nirikshan's largest Indian customers had, during their 2025 renewals, asked for the telemetry restriction that the 2023 deal had pioneered.

Internationally, Nirikshan's exposure ran through two channels. In North America, Nikhil Chandran sold to mid-market food-processing and logistics operators out of New Jersey, at contract values roughly three times Indian ones and with a sales cycle twice as long. In the Gulf, the company's largest single account was Rukn Facilities Services, a Dubai-headquartered facilities-management group with 27,000 staff across the UAE, Oman and Saudi Arabia, on a contract worth ₹18 crore a year that came up for renewal on 31 August 2026. Rukn's renewal had one stated condition, repeated in three separate emails: a customer-facing "Plant Health" analytics module that would let Rukn's own account directors show their clients, weekly, what had been inspected and what had been fixed.

4. The situation in detail

March 2025. Nirikshan adopted a commercial product-analytics SDK in the multi-tenant app. The belief was that the company now had instrumentation. Events were defined by whichever squad shipped a feature; by June 2026 the taxonomy had 412 event names, of which 61 had been fired at least once in the last thirty days and eleven accounted for 94 percent of volume.

August 2025. Rhea Mathew joined in Toronto as Head of Data and began publishing a monthly "usage health" report from the SDK. The report showed monthly active technicians rising from 38,000 to 51,000 over the year, and was quoted in the Series C materials raised in November. What has since turned out to be wrong is a sampling setting: the SDK had been installed with a 50 percent client-side sample on session events for devices on metered connections, a default that nobody changed and that Rhea discovered in April 2026. The trend direction survives the correction; the level does not.

November 2025. Two renewals were lost, together worth ₹7.4 crore. Both accounts had shown green on the customer-success health score in the preceding quarter. The post-mortem found that in one case the plant had moved three of four checklist categories back to paper after a supervisor transfer, and in the other the customer had been using Nirikshan for statutory records only, which was a small fraction of the contracted scope and had looked healthy because statutory records are filed reliably every single day.

January 2026. Sarita Iyengar proposed usage-based pricing for FY27: a base platform fee plus a per-active-technician charge, which would align the company's revenue with deployment depth and, she argued, add ₹22–28 crore of ARR at no sales cost. The proposal assumed a trustworthy count of active technicians.

March 2026. Girish asked for the weekly dashboard. Aparna's team built it in six weeks, with fourteen tiles chosen by asking each leader what they wanted to see. The belief was that the dashboard would create the review. What has turned out to be wrong is the direction of causation: there was no standing Tuesday meeting with a decision attached to it, so the dashboard became a page, and a page competes with a spreadsheet that arrives by email.

April 2026. Rhea's team built a second, independent count of active technicians directly from the application database — any user account that had submitted at least one checklist record or work-order update in the period — reasoning that server-side records were authoritative and could not be sampled away. The two counts diverged, and a third arrived in May when Meenal Joshi's customer-success team assembled seat-utilisation figures from the quarterly business reviews, in which customers state their own numbers. Exhibit 3 sets all three side by side.

June 2026. Rukn's chief operating officer wrote to say that the renewal would proceed on the existing commercial terms only if the Plant Health module was in production by 30 November. Nikhil Chandran forwarded the email to the leadership list with the subject line changed to "Not a feature request."

8. The options as Aparna sees them

Aparna had spent the weekend arranging and rearranging three options, and had begun to notice that the arrangement kept pushing the same awkward fact off the page.

Option A: fix the instrument. Give the September squad to the instrumentation rebuild, adopt the application-database definition, publish a restatement of the FY26 active-technician series, and reconcile the three counts at account level before the rate card is frozen. This gives Sarita a number she can price on and gives the product organisation, for the first time, a series it can trust. It costs the company the Plant Health module in the September quarter, which means telling Rukn in July that a 30 November date is not achievable — or promising it and building it in the December quarter with a team that does not yet exist.

Option B: build what the customer is paying for. Give the squad to Plant Health, secure the ₹18 crore renewal and the North American pipeline behind it, and run FY27 on the numbers the company already has with their weaknesses documented. The counter-argument is that Plant Health is an aggregation of exactly the data whose definitions are in dispute, so the company would be shipping to its largest customer a weekly report built on a metric it cannot reconcile internally — and that a customer-facing dashboard creates an obligation to be right that an internal one does not.

Option C: shrink the dashboard and change the meeting. Spend no engineering at all. Cut the fourteen tiles to three, give each an owner, and attach them to a standing Tuesday decision — pricing, renewal triage, roadmap — on the theory that the problem in Exhibit 1 is not the tiles but the absence of a meeting that needs them. This is free, can be done by Friday, and leaves both the reconciliation and the Rukn commitment exactly where they are.

What Aparna keeps writing in the margin and not putting on the slide is that all three options treat the dashboard as an artefact to be improved, and that the two facts which most govern the company's FY27 are not artefacts at all: that 34 percent of revenue is contractually unmeasurable and growing, and that the segment which looks best on the numbers the company does have is the segment where it has lost the most money. A dashboard that showed those two facts honestly would have fewer tiles than Girish wants and would answer none of the questions Sarita needs answered by August.

Engineering has one squad of six engineers and one designer free from 1 September and no budget for contractors; Tanmay has stated in writing that he will not split it. The company held ₹88 crore of cash in June against a net burn of ₹2.1 crore a month and a board mandate to reach operating break-even by Q4 FY28. The nineteen single-tenant contracts contain a no-telemetry undertaking with no unilateral exit; renegotiating even one requires opening a commercial conversation that legal has advised against doing before renewal. Log retention on the sync service is 400 days, which means any backfill of the database series before June 2025 becomes impossible after this quarter. Under the DPDP Act, technician-level data is personal data, and any customer-facing module that names individual technicians requires a purpose-limitation review that compliance has estimated at three weeks and has not yet started.
